bridge: D05 introduced log evidence. Use fictional intelligence notes and the supplied technique descriptions.
teaching:
### Distinguish an indicator from a behaviour

An indicator might be a file hash, address or domain connected with observed activity. Its meaning can change as infrastructure or software changes. A behaviour describes what an actor did, such as creating a scheduled task for persistence.

### Use ATT&CK as a description aid

MITRE ATT&CK organises documented adversary behaviours into techniques and related information. Mapping evidence to a technique can help communicate what was observed. It does not prove that a particular named actor caused the event or that the organisation detects every variation.

### Check the intelligence's basis

Ask who reported it, what they observed, when it occurred and how confidently they made the association. Separate direct evidence from inference. A popular report can still be incomplete for your environment.

### Connect it with a decision

Would this information change a search, detection rule, containment choice or collection plan? State that use and its limits. Do not automatically block all traffic associated with a shared service based on one unexplained indicator.

In the exercise, link each claimed behaviour with the synthetic event that supports it and write what additional evidence would strengthen or challenge the mapping.

For the E2 case in Practise, the supplied facts are: evidence E2; host H; 09:01 UTC; command ipconfig /all. That command can collect network configuration information. Compare the documented definition of ATT&CK T1016, System Network Configuration Discovery, with those facts. Legitimate troubleshooting is a possible benign explanation. The command name alone does not prove malicious intent or identify an actor.
example:
Synthetic note
Observation: source event E1 records process X reading file F at 09:00 UTC.
Interpretation: file access occurred under the recorded identity.
Not established: malicious intent, tool family, data exfiltration.
Candidate mapping: only after behaviour meets the selected technique definition.
Record: ATT&CK version, definition link, evidence IDs and uncertainty.
explanation: This deliberately weak observation demonstrates restraint. Mapping a file read to a specific adversary technique without supporting context can overstate the evidence. Conversely, uncertainty should be documented rather than replacing all analysis with a vague label.
exercise: For E1 in the supplied note, fill observed/inferred/unknown columns. Then use the complete E2 case taught in Learn: ipconfig /all on host H at 09:01 UTC. Write a mapping with evidence id, behaviour, technique id/name, definition source/date and one benign alternative. Use https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1016/ as the definition reference. The provider handout is optional additional practice; no command execution is needed.
solution: E1: observed file read under the recorded identity; interpretation limited to that read; unknown intent, human actor, tool family and transfer contents. A specific adversary technique is not established. E2: cite the exact command line and host/time, describe network-configuration discovery, map cautiously to T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery and record the definition version/date you consult (version 1.7, modified 12 May 2026 when checked on 31 October 2026). Routine troubleshooting is a benign alternative. No actor or exfiltration attribution follows from either event.
challenge: For a fresh fictional report “X ran on host H; a log confirms an outbound connection, but no content capture exists,” state what is observed and what would be needed to assert data exfiltration. Propose a cautious mapping workflow.
challenge_solution: Process execution and a connection are observations under the stated logs. Exfiltration requires evidence of data movement/context beyond mere connectivity. Consult the current technique definition, cite evidence, mark confidence and identify missing telemetry.
